chunks: I was informed by the Sheikh Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Nuʿman, may God have mercy on him, who said: I was informed by Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Walid, from his father, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar; and Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ʿIsa and al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban; from al-Husayn ibn Saʿid, from Ibn Abi ʿUmayr, from Abu Ayyub, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu ʿAbd Allah (peace be upon him):

that he was asked about water in which animals urinate, dogs lap, and from which a person in a state of major ritual impurity (junub) bathes. He said: If the water is the measure of a kurr, nothing renders it impure.

key_terms.الدَّوَابُّ: dawabb — beasts, four-legged animals (here contextually those urinating in water)
key_terms.الْجُنُبُ: junub — a person in a state of major ritual impurity (janaba) requiring ghusl before prayer
key_terms.كُرٍّ: kurr — a unit of water volume in Shia fiqh (approx. 377 litres); water below this threshold is susceptible to ritual impurity
key_terms.يُنَجِّسْهُ: renders it ritually impure (Form II verb from najasa; najasah = ritual impurity)

ai.seo_question: What is the minimum volume of water (kurr) that cannot be rendered ritually impure by anything, according to Imam al-Sadiq in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam Jaʿfar al-Sadiq (peace be upon him), transmitted through a lengthy chain of reliable Shia narrators, establishes the foundational ruling on water purity. The Imam rules that once water reaches the volume of a kurr (a standard measure in Shia fiqh, approximately 377 litres), it cannot be rendered ritually impure by animals urinating in it, dogs lapping from it, or a person in a state of major ritual impurity (junub) bathing in it. This ruling is the cornerstone of the chapter on water quantity in al-Istibsar and is cited across all four major Shia hadith collections.
